content: Telomeric repeat-binding factor 1 (TERF1) is a protein encoded by the TERF1 gene in humans. The TERF1 gene is located on chromosome 8, specifically at the region spanning 73,921,097 to 73,960,357 base pairs. This gene produces two alternatively spliced transcripts. TERF1 is also referred to by other names, including TRF, PIN2 (Proteinase Inhibitor 2), TRF1, t-TRF1, and h-TRF1-AS. The TERF1 protein has a distinct structure, which includes a C-terminal Myb motif, a dimerization domain near its N-terminus, and an acidic N-terminal region. Subcellularly, TERF1 is distributed across various cellular compartments, including the nucleoplasm, chromosomes, telomeric regions, the nuclear telomere cap complex, the cytoplasm, the spindle, the nucleus, the nucleolus, and nuclear chromosomes. TERF1 plays a critical role as a telomere-specific protein and is a component of the telomere nucleoprotein complex. It is present at telomeres throughout the cell cycle and functions as an inhibitor of telomerase. By acting in cis, it limits the elongation of individual chromosome ends. TERF1 protects mammalian telomeres from DNA repair mechanisms and regulates telomerase activity. This protein is essential for monitoring cellular aging, as the progressive loss of telomeric ends is a key mechanism in human cellular aging. TERF1 binds to telomere ends and is a part of the shelterin nucleoprotein complex. It inhibits telomerase, an enzyme that elongates chromosomes by adding TTAGGG sequences to their ends. TERF1 acts as a cis-regulatory element, preventing excessive elongation of chromosome ends by telomerase. Structurally, TERF1 contains a dimerization domain near its amino terminus, a carboxyl-terminal tail (a free carboxyl group at the end of the protein chain), and an acidic amino terminus (a free amine group at the start of the protein chain). TERF1 is involved in several biological processes. It plays a role in the cellular response to drugs and negatively regulates telomere maintenance during semi-conservative replication. It also positively regulates microtubule polymerization and mitosis, as well as the mitotic cell cycle. Additionally, TERF1 is involved in cell division and negatively regulates telomere maintenance mediated by telomerase. Beyond its role as a telomerase inhibitor, TERF1 facilitates protein homodimerization, DNA binding, protein heterodimerization, and microtubule binding. It also binds to telomeric DNA, double-stranded telomeric DNA, chromatin, and participates in DNA bending. In colorectal cancer, TERF1 protein levels correlate with telomere length. Telomeres protect chromosomes from degradation and end-to-end fusion. The progressive loss of telomeric ends is a key factor in cellular aging. In a study analyzing TRF1 protein concentrations and their relationship with telomere length and telomerase activity in tumor and normal colorectal mucosa, high levels of TRF1 were observed in 68.7% of tumor samples. In contrast, most normal samples exhibited negative or weak TRF1 concentrations. Among tumor samples, telomere length was significantly associated with TRF1 protein levels. This suggests that TRF1 is an important factor in tumor progression and may serve as a diagnostic marker. The TERF1 protein interacts with several other proteins, including: SALL1 (Sal-like 1, a transcription factor), ABL (Abelson murine leukemia viral oncogene homolog, a tyrosine kinase), MAPRE2 (Microtubule-associated protein RP/EB), ATM (Ataxia telangiectasia mutated, a protein kinase involved in DNA damage response), PINX1 (TERF1-interacting telomerase inhibitor 1), TINF2 (TERF1-interacting nuclear factor), TNKS2 (Tankyrase 2, a poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase enzyme), and NME1 (Nucleoside diphosphate kinase 1). In summary, TERF1 is a multifunctional protein with critical roles in telomere maintenance, cellular aging, and tumor progression. Its interactions with various proteins and its regulatory functions make it a key player in cellular and molecular processes.
